title: Conditional Independence and the Constraint Equations of Information: Derivation, Closure, and Natural-Gradient Dynamics of the Four Functionals
abstract: This paper studies the constraint equations of systems satisfying "unknown information is determined solely by known information" (conditional independence I(τ;K∣p)=0I(τ;K∣p)=0). The set of premises consists of Postulate 1 (conditional independence, the sufficiency postulate), Postulate 2 (stationarity, the mathematical form of information conservation), and the normative condition (A) (emission injectivity); beyond the two postulates and (A) no further substantive assumption is introduced, and the modeling conventions (product convention, direction convention (C1), metric axiom) are flagged explicitly in Sections 3.1 and 4.3. The derivation proceeds in four steps. First, the premises yield the machine structure and the three conservation identities. Second, per-structure decomposition yields the four core functionals (defined in Section 5): HH (the integrand of the entropy rate), II (the per-structure component of the one-step mutual information), and ΔSΔS and AA (the measure of the antisymmetric half and the symmetric half of the forward/backward comparison structure). Third, framework-internal closure: within the decomposition framework built from Shannon entropy and KL divergence, and given the choice of metrics, there are exactly these four core functionals — "core functionals" refers to the per-structure integrands and the two-half components appearing in the decomposition identities, which does not exclude nonlinear constructible quantities (the decomposition structure provides four positions, single-cell Shannon-lattice closure excludes a fifth component, and closure at the pair and ensemble levels is a conjecture); the paper claims no unconditional completeness over arbitrary families of functionals. Fourth, the learning dynamics is the natural gradient flow on the statistical manifold. Functional independence of the four functionals is proved on an example family (Appendix B) and open for general families. The four functionals have different statuses: HH and II are relatively intrinsic (formulas fixed by uniqueness theorems); ΔSΔS is fixed by the one-sided KL divergence selected by the zero-set requirement, additivity, and the data-processing inequality; AA is normalized as JS/ln⁡2JS/ln2 by the metric axiom, and its cross-system form requires a pair of distributions (three intrinsic functionals plus one cross-system functional). The derivation does not rely on exponential families (which are optional structure). The constraint equations hold universally within the scope of conditional independence; semantic regularities lie outside this boundary. title: Enhanced Short-Text Clustering Based on a Multirepresentation Fusion Model
abstract: Short-text clustering has become increasingly important because of the exponential growth of textual data. However, traditional methods struggle with sparsity, limited context, and poor cluster cohesion. Recently, innovations have made word embedding algorithms, including Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText, available for effectively learn semantic relationships. Although these methods have advantages, they tend to concentrate on semantics area. These limitations are addressed in this study by adopting an enhanced short-text clustering method based on multirepresentation. Specifically, this study integrates heterogeneous embeddings into a unified framework using weighted L2-normalized concatenation, followed by Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-based dimensionality reduction that retains 95% of the variance, thereby create a unified semantic representation. Unlike simple concatenation approaches of embeddings, pre-space normalization operations are added before the fusion operation to avoid the presence of dominant embedding bias. The proposed model was evaluated on four benchmark datasets, namely, StackOverflow, AgNews, BioASQ, and SearchSnippet, via the k-means and k-medoids clustering algorithms. The results demonstrate substantial improvements in the clustering quality metrics. Compared with the results of the baseline models Bag of Words (BoW)/Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), the average gains were statistically significant: 29% in silhouette score, 8% in adjusted Rand index, and 8% in normalized mutual information over the best (single) embedding baseline (GloVe with k-medoids) and 63%, 35%, and 40%, respectively, over traditional BoW/TF-IDF methods. Most improvements are found to be statistically significant at p < 0.05. Additionally, PCA was applied to reduce noise and dimensionality, potentially improving clustering outcomes. title: Empowerment Gain as Causal Learning, Causal Learning as Empowerment Gain: A Bridge between Bayesian Causal Hypothesis Testing and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract Cognitive scientists have applied advances in our formal understanding of causation in philosophy and computer science, particularly within the Causal Bayes Net formalism, to understand human causal learning. In parallel, reinforcement learning (RL) researchers have developed the idea of an intrinsic reward signal called “empowerment.” An agent is rewarded for maximizing the mutual information between its actions and their outcomes, regardless of the external reward value of those outcomes. Empowerment may be an important bridge between classical Bayesian causal learning and RL and may help to characterize causal learning in humans and enable it in machines.

title: From Perception to Prediction and Intervention: Benchmarking Proactive Video Assistants in Real-Life Scenarios
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction and intervention. We benchmark 12 representative open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems. Our evaluation shows that current models struggle to make well-calibrated response decisions. Finally, we construct additional proactive training data and train \textsc{P$^3$I-Assistant-4B}, achieving improvements on several tasks, though gains remain uneven across capabilities. Together, these findings show that effective proactive assistance requires not only visual understanding, but also precise response timing and appropriate restraint.

title: Parallel Repetition for Entangled Games via Conditional Relative Entropy
abstract: We give a proof of the cubic parallel-repetition bound for finite two-player entangled games using quantum conditional relative entropy. For a game with entangled value $1-\varepsilon<1$ and answer alphabets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, its $n$-fold repeated value is at most \[ \exp[-Ω(\varepsilon^3n/L)],\qquad L:=\max\{1,\log(|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|)\}, \] for every $n\ge1$. This recovers Song's cubic rate. We also prove a threshold bound: the probability of winning a fraction at least $1-\varepsilon+δ$ is at most $\exp[-Ω(δ^5n/(\varepsilon^2L))]$ for $0<δ\le\varepsilon$. Our information charge is the decrease in relative entropy when a question reference is discarded. Our comparison states preserve the original conditional question law. A chain rule bounds the coordinate charges using the cost of conditioning on checked wins and retaining checked answers. Our main lemma converts small charges into nearby pure-state descriptions and local corrections, each depending only on one player's question. Together with Song's sampler, these enable approximate local preparation of the conditioned workspace.

title: Semantic Latent Alignment for Flow Matching with Invertible Bi-Lipschitz Adapters
abstract: Pretrained latent spaces trade compression, reconstruction, and the learnability of the coordinates a downstream generator has to work in, which complicates adapting these spaces to different domains or tasks: continued training is expensive, and without a new alignment objective it often fails to improve downstream generation. We instead leave the encoder and decoder fixed and change only the coordinates between them, using an invertible bi-Lipschitz adapter aligned offline to a semantic teacher and frozen during class-conditional flow matching. Invertibility preserves compatibility with the pretrained autoencoder, while the bi-Lipschitz constraint limits how far alignment can distort its latent geometry. This provides a simple way to improve semantic organization while retaining the compression and reconstruction properties of the original latent space. On two medical imaging datasets, constrained latent adaptation improves feature metrics, seed stability and counterfactual edit strength, while remaining competitive on downstream classification. In contrast, unconstrained adaptation can become highly anisotropic and sensitive despite remaining invertible, highlighting the importance of controlling geometric distortion. Our results suggest that carefully constrained post-hoc adaptation offers a parameter-efficient and tuning-free alternative to jointly modifying the representation during generative training.

title: Spectral theory of energy-selective quantum search with Ising Hamiltonian phase oracles
abstract: We develop an exact spectral-response theory for the Grover-type iterate \(W_T=D_ξ\exp(-\ii T H)\), in which the evolution generated by a diagonal Ising Hamiltonian is used directly as a continuous phase oracle. An energy-grouped recurrence and its generating-function solution show how the empirical characteristic function determines the position, width, height, and saturation time of an energy-selective resonance. For an annealed Gaussian density of states, a high-density-tail resonance containing \(M\) configurations is reached after \(Θ(\sqrt{2^n/M})\) oracle calls with success probability \(Θ(1)\), giving a quadratic query improvement over independent uniform sampling with classical energy evaluation. For correlated random Ising spectra, overlap-dependent covariances lead to a realization-dependent resonance shift with root-mean-square scale \(O(n^{-3})\), parametrically larger than the resonance width, and can also reduce the peak height. The shift is both an algorithmic detuning and a coherent probe of sample-specific spectral fluctuations whose ensemble statistics reflect the Ising overlap structure. Spectral symmetrization and iterative calibration can remove or compensate the resonance-center displacement for prescribed-energy targeting. We also clarify the relation to designed spectral filters and the precision and coherence requirements of this asymptotic primitive.

title: Teaching a Lightweight Neural TTS Engine to Read: Span-Preserving Text Preparation, Phoneme-Set-Aware Pronunciation Repair and Model-Timed Subtitles for Piper
abstract: Piper is a widely used neural text-to-speech engine that runs in real time on ordinary processors. It reads text through the espeak-ng phonemizer and performs no text normalization of its own, so written forms such as prices, dates, abbreviations, units and phone numbers are often read literally. We describe a text preparation layer for Piper that rewrites such forms while keeping, for every spoken word, the span of the written text it came from; it also segments text into sentences, lines, paragraphs and clauses with explicit pauses. We report two further observations: several community English (US) Piper voices were trained on espeak's British phoneme set and therefore pronounce words such as schedule and privacy the British way, which we repair with phoneme strings restricted to the symbols those voices were trained on; and Piper's duration output yields exact word timings for subtitles once spoken words are mapped back to written words with a small dynamic programme. On a suite of 84 hand-written English and Spanish test sentences the phoneme error rate against reference readings fell from 32.6% to 0.9%, false sentence endings fell from 18 to 0, and none of 19 control sentences changed. On a held-out half of NVIDIA NeMo's public text normalization test cases, which we did not write, the phoneme error rate was 41.0% for unprocessed text, 28.5% for a typical number-to-words script and 15.8% for our layer in English (200 cases), and 64.7%, 56.2% and 43.2% in Spanish (277 cases). We release the code and evaluation data under the Apache License 2.0. Files: the paper (English) and the study package, which contains the ttsprep text preparation layer with its unit tests and Piper timing adapter (Apache License 2.0), the evaluation scripts, the 103 test sentences with references, the NeMo test cases with their source and licence, all result files, the LaTeX sources and the paper in English and Spanish. Web version in English and Spanish: https://loudness.ai/research/piper-tts-text-normalization/ (technical report LA-RB-2026-002, version 1.0.1). Version 1.0.1 corrects one misprinted character in the PDF (the ordinal “10.º”); nothing else changed.

title: Building a domain-specific large language model for Chinese ancient books: a case study on epitaph modelling
abstract: Introduction. With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence technology, large language models (LLMs) are expected to play an important role in improving access to and the use of library collections. This study constructs and develops a generative conversational large language model tailored specifically to epitaphs, overcoming traditional research paths and systems of digitisation. Method. Based on the Chinese epitaph database built by the Zhejiang University Library and some commercial epitaph databases, an epitaph generative dialogue large language model was constructed using Doubao as the base model through pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and other full process trainings. Analysis. This study used human evaluation, in which experts, researchers, or general users assessed the quality of model-generated outputs. The evaluation included the epitaphs of Cui Yi, Liu Yi, and Lihua in the Tang dynasty. Results. The model successfully performed intelligent interpretation of epitaphs, automatic information extraction, and other knowledge-based services, thereby providing new ideas for constructing an ancient literature corpus from excavated materials represented by epitaphs. Conclusion. A large-scale domain-specific foundational model tailored for library applications was successfully developed. The study offers innovative approaches for processing historical texts and suggests new directions for AI integration in library knowledge systems.

title: Structural Invariant Framework (SIF 1.0): a registry-based framework for empirically verified terminology preservation in neural EN→UA translation of metrological standards
abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) can produce fluent output while systematically deforming domain-critical terminology in metrological standards. Under GUM (JCGM 100:2008) Annex D.1.1, an incomplete definition of the measurand is a possible source of measurement uncertainty; terminological corruption in normative translation can therefore propagate metrologically consequential error into downstream interpretation and decisions. We present the Structural Invariant Framework (SIF 1.0), a protocol-verified five-layer architecture that detects, classifies, and enforces canonical anchor forms in EN→UA NMT output for metrological standards. SIF does not target general fluency; it asks whether defined structural invariants are preserved. The framework contributes: (i) a taxonomy of six deformation types and two subtypes, derived from 183 annotated corpus rows based on JCGM 106:2012, GUM, and related vocabulary standards; (ii) the 22-term Anchor Registry, a control object implementing Registry Supremacy by defining admissible terminology for a specified document family; and (iii) deterministic Layer 4 enforcement. On a frozen set of 35 sentences (26 anchor-bearing and 9 null probes), detection recall was 1,000 and the false-positive rate was 0,000. Layer 4 raised Anchor Identity Precision, computed over anchor positions, from 0,1905 for the unmodified Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-uk baseline to 0,7143 (+ 52,4 percentage points). The neural bridge remained a pilot and was not used in these results. Evidence from the frozen corpus, expert-elicited probes, and authentic JCGM documents supports the directional claim that, in the evaluated configuration, Registry-based deterministic enforcement is more reliable than learned generation for preserving controlled terminology.

evidence.title: Structural Invariant Framework (SIF 1.0): a registry-based framework for empirically verified terminology preservation in neural EN→UA translation of metrological standards
evidence.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) can produce fluent output while systematically deforming domain-critical terminology in metrological standards. Under GUM (JCGM 100:2008) Annex D.1.1, an incomplete definition of the measurand is a possible source of measurement uncertainty; terminological corruption in normative translation can therefore propagate metrologically consequential error into downstream interpretation and decisions. We present the Structural Invariant Framework (SIF 1.0), a protocol-verified five-layer architecture that detects, classifies, and enforces canonical anchor forms in EN→UA NMT output for metrological standards. SIF does not target general fluency; it asks whether defined structural invariants are preserved. The framework contributes: (i) a taxonomy of six deformation types and two subtypes, derived from 183 annotated corpus rows based on JCGM 106:2012, GUM, and related vocabulary standards; (ii) the 22-term Anchor Registry, a control object implementing Registry Supremacy by defining admissible terminology for a specified document family; and (iii) deterministic Layer 4 enforcement. On a frozen set of 35 sentences (26 anchor-bearing and 9 null probes), detection recall was 1,000 and the false-positive rate was 0,000. Layer 4 raised Anchor Identity Precision, computed over anchor positions, from 0,1905 for the unmodified Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-uk baseline to 0,7143 (+ 52,4 percentage points). The neural bridge remained a pilot and was not used in these results. Evidence from the frozen corpus, expert-elicited probes, and authentic JCGM documents supports the directional claim that, in the evaluated configuration, Registry-based deterministic enforcement is more reliable than learned generation for preserving controlled terminology.

title: Meta-Learning-Based Few-Shot Membership Inference Attacks Under Restricted Black-Box Access to Ranked Top-K Probabilities
abstract: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) determine whether a sample was used to train a target model. Existing attacks often require abundant auxiliary data or many reference models, which may be unavailable in restricted services. We propose a meta-learning-based few-shot MIA for black-box interfaces returning only ranked Top-K probabilities. Shadow-model responses form episodic tasks for a relation network; at inference, ten known target members are aggregated as support and compared with each query. Across six directed dataset–architecture transfers, descriptive mean AUCs range from 0.8115 to 0.9471. In the primary Mini-ImageNet/ResNet-18 to CIFAR-100/ViT-B/16 transfer, three independent target/relation-network pipelines achieve an AUC of 0.9444±0.0061 and a TPR of 0.0998±0.0455 at 1% FPR. Performance is competitive with raw Top-1 (0.9435±0.0036) and few-shot-fine-tuned Shokri (0.9420±0.0022), with no uniform dominance. Reducing the target’s member–held-out accuracy gap from 77.17 to 18.53 percentage points lowers AUC to 0.6038±0.0094. Support and relation-function controls also vary by initialization. Thus, ranked Top-K outputs can leak membership information, particularly for overfitted targets, while learned support conditioning provides no universal advantage.

title: PharmAI: domain-specific QA generation by adaptive learning and fine-tuning of small language models
abstract: Background Domain-specific medical question-answering (QA) models face bottlenecks due to scarce labeled data, specialized terminology, and constrained computational hardware. Objectives The study aims to develop an efficient pharmaceutical question-answering (QA) system that can be trained and deployed on consumer-grade hardware using Small Language Models (SLMs). Materials and methods The pipeline processes four pharmaceutical textbooks containing 3,977 total pages, producing 7,370 semantically similar text chunks and 2,144 synthetic QA pairs under four questioning categories: definition, mechanism, comparison, and clinical application. Three Small Language Models (SLMs), namely SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5–1.5B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2–1B-Instruct, are fine-tuned under the same QLoRA (Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation) configurations and then evaluated with retrieval metrics (Recall@K, Mean Reciprocal Rank) and generation metrics (ROUGE-1/2/L, Semantic Similarity, BERTScore). Architectural decisions including NF4 4-bit quantization, CPU-based FAISS indexing, and completion-only loss masking are implemented due to hardware constraints and validated via ablation analysis. Results SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5–1.5B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2–1B-Instruct demonstrated identical retrieval performance, achieving a Recall@1 of 0.517, Recall@3 of 0.732, Recall@5 of 0.797, and an MRR of 0.628. Similarly, the generation performance evaluation revealed that Qwen2.5–1.5B FT outperformed the other fine-tuned SLMs, achieving the highest scores across all metrics (ROUGE-1 = 0.47, ROUGE-2 = 0.25, ROUGE-L = 0.38, and BERTScore = 0.72). In comparison, SmolLM2-1.7B FT and Llama-3.2–1B FT exhibited comparable performance, with ROUGE-1 scores of approximately 0.35, ROUGE-2 scores of 0.16–0.17, ROUGE-L scores of 0.25–0.26, and BERTScores of 0.66, indicating lower lexical and semantic alignment with the reference outputs than Qwen2.5–1.5B FT. Conclusion We evaluate retrieval and generation performance using comprehensive metric suites, incorporating a category-wise breakdown that reveals comparison questions to be the most challenging for single-passage retrieval architectures.

title: d-wave superconductivity in quintuple-layer bulk superconductor La_6Ni_5O_{12}
abstract: The recent realization of bulk superconductivity in the quintuple-layer nickelate La_6Ni_5O_{12} opens new opportunities to probe the pairing symmetry of the reduced Ruddlesden--Popper (RP) nickelate family. Using an effective five-layer Hubbard model and variational Monte Carlo calculations, we find that a spin-singlet d_{x^2-y^2}-wave state is energetically favored, while extended-s-wave pairing is strongly suppressed. Based on the optimized superconducting state, we further calculate several experimentally accessible observables. The tunneling density of states exhibits a characteristic V-shaped low-energy spectrum, the superfluid density shows a linear low-temperature depletion, the Knight shift decreases below T_c, and the spin-lattice relaxation rate follows 1/T_1Tpropto T^2, together providing consistent signatures of a clean nodal superconductor. Extending the same framework to related reduced RP nickelates, we find a robust d-wave tendency in infinite-layer LaNiO_{2}, while trilayer La_4Ni_3O_{8} at its nominal filling lies close to the boundary between d-wave superconductivity and a non-superconducting state. These results establish bulk La_6Ni_5O_{12} as a promising platform for determining the pairing symmetry of nickelate superconductors and suggest a common d_{x^2-y^2}-wave pairing tendency across the reduced RP nickelate family.

title: Change the Number, Change the Answer: Assessing Rating Scale Sensitivity in LLM-Based Text Scoring
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.

title: Anvil: Scaling Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Knowledge Recirculation
abstract: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.

title: Superconducting circuits host two-level systems with lifetimes exceeding one second
abstract: Understanding the microscopic environment of superconducting qubits is a central challenge for quantum technologies. Parasitic two-level systems (TLSs) of various microscopic origins are ubiquitous and limit qubit performance through decoherence, frequency drifts, and leakage. Recently, long-lived TLSs with lifetimes exceeding those of state-of-the-art qubits have been shown to induce correlated qubit dynamics, with direct implications for quantum error correction. Here, we perform wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmon qubits and identify microscopic degrees of freedom that outlive the qubit by orders of magnitude. Pump-probe measurements at varying detunings from these objects reveal intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second. Their weak coupling to the qubit, in the kilohertz range, is consistent with positional defects described by the standard tunneling model, without excluding other microscopic origins such as magnetic spin impurities or trapped quasiparticles. More broadly, these results establish superconducting qubits as a sensitive probe of exceptionally long-lived microscopic degrees of freedom and open a route toward their controlled access and functionalization.

title: VoteGEO-Bench: Measuring the Impact of Generative Engine Optimization on Electoral Visibility
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for election information, yet little is known about how external web content shapes the political information they present. Generative engine optimization (GEO) rewrites web content to improve its visibility in generated responses. To investigate its potential risks in voting scenarios (VoteGEO), we introduce VoteGEO-Bench, a benchmark covering the 2024 U.S. presidential election and the 2026 Japanese House of Representatives election, combining election-related queries, historical webpages, and voter personas. We first analyze sources cited by generative engines and find that many citations come from lower-cost owned and open-platform sources, while some webpages remain visible across days. We then evaluate 11 rewriting strategies in 4 categories, examining target specification, effectiveness across engines and elections, and the role of voter personas. Rewriting without specifying a target rarely increases target exposure, whereas target-specified rewriting more often does. Strategies that improve page organization or strengthen a position through argumentation yield greater gains than adding supporting evidence or changing wording. For the two strongest strategies, gains remain broadly positive across evaluated U.S. personas, but persona conditioning shows no consistent effect on these gains. Explicit partisan identities can create baseline exposure gaps larger than the gain from rewriting one webpage. When partisanship is implicit in the voter profile, baseline shifts depend on how strongly the engine responds to that signal.

title: A One-Sided McDiarmid-Type Inequality for Heavy Tails via Reverse KL Tensorization
abstract: We revisit McDiarmid's inequality, a central tool in statistical learning theory and algorithm analysis. We show that large deviations above the mean are exponentially unlikely for functions of independent random variables that are almost surely bounded above and satisfy a conditional moment assumption of order $p\in(1,2]$. When $p<2$, the result applies even when the function has infinite variance. Our proof relies on a new tensorization inequality for the Kullback--Leibler divergence, termed reverse KL tensorization, which may be of independent interest. Applications include concentration of the sample mean and median-of-means estimator, and one-sided uniform risk bounds for unbounded losses.

title: Vocabulary-constrained rewriting and translation for dictionary-based sign language avatars, system outputs, scores and analyses
abstract: Underlying data of a study on dictionary-based sign language avatars, which play a recorded sign for each word in their dictionary and fingerspell the other content words. The study measures how much an International Sign avatar with several hundred signs fingerspells in English meeting transcripts (AMI Meeting Corpus) and written sentences (FLORES-200), and whether rewording the text, or translating text from Greek, French, Spanish and German, into words that the avatar can sign avoids the fingerspelling without changing the meaning. The deposit holds the output of every method for every sentence and segment, with its computing time, the scores of every sentence (signing plan, COMET, chrF, cosine similarity and mutual entailment) and their summaries, the tables of the article and the complete results with bootstrap confidence intervals, the extension of the IS dictionary with frequent words and the ranked list of the words it lacks, the failure analyses of restricted rewriting (look-alike words, unwanted country names and dropped stop-list words), and the sample and the clip statistics of the IS dictionary. README.md describes every file and lists the files under CC BY-SA 4.0, which are those that contain FLORES-200 sentences or outputs derived from them. The other files are under CC BY 4.0. The code is at https://github.com/ntantaroudas/constrained-translation-sign-avatar.

title: Code and data for Compositional generation of robot mission admission conditions from incomplete execution evidence
abstract: Reproducibility materials for a compositional method that constructs coupled resource-bound conditions and unresolved execution obligations from a finite robot task, executor semantics and incomplete local evidence. This deposit contains scientific code, data, frozen protocols, raw results and reproduction explanations; the manuscript and supplementary manuscript are excluded. Historical archives retain the software and native evidence studies. S22 adds direct-query and direct-row construction baselines, an implemented homogeneous-repetition reduction and independent extended-LP checks. Direct-row construction is near parity with the proposed sequential adapter; the 30-repeat resource example is reduced from 496 inequalities to three. S23 adds eighteen native calibration jobs and twelve held-out ArduCopter SITL executions on six fresh route identities. For a current batch requiring one of three speed domains, the measured calibration job-set wall cost is 89.03 seconds rather than 253.36 seconds for full-library acquisition. The equally informed direct baseline requests the same jobs and obtains the same saving. Thirty-six correlated budget scores include two narrow boundary failures; all twelve admitted conditions succeed, while 22 successful conditions remain unadmitted. These are empirical simulator-local results, not physical safety certification or a claim of a new controller. S24 adds one constructed structural instance: a raw branching and repeated task from which a bounded frontend generates 35 execution obligations, six sealed supplementation, repair, revision and refresh states, twelve structural controls, a separate complete-path reference, and eighteen deterministic planar-model probes. It demonstrates that a branch whose resource inequality is redundant still carries its completion obligation, and that a task edit invalidates exactly the claims that depend on it. The surrounding directory is the S22 scaffolding the instance reuses. S25 adds the sealed shared-instance comparison with the closest published admission framework: the backend obligation layer of the authors' publicly released EAMSR modules (tag v2.0.0-r1, commit f42cc53) is run on the frozen structural instance for six stages and both permitted paths, with clauses supplied directly from a pre-registered mapping table, a completed record table, and a sensitivity variant for the released low-state-of-charge energy term. The admission-decision layer of that package is not implemented and is outside the executed comparison. Author-owned software is MIT licensed. Author-owned data, protocols and reproduction explanations are CC BY 4.0. Third-party licenses and external runtime requirements remain as documented. The public subset omits manuscript and rendered publication assets; retained scientific code and data bytes are unchanged and archive provenance is recorded.

title: Adaptive Self–Mutual Distillation in Multi-Agent Learning: A State-Driven Switching Framework
abstract: Knowledge distillation enables learning systems to transfer informative predictive distributions, intermediate representations, or relational knowledge from one learning process to another. Two relevant paradigms are self-distillation, in which a model learns from its own historical, intermediate, or alternative representations, and mutual distillation, in which multiple models exchange knowledge during training. Although these paradigms have complementary properties, committing to either one throughout training can be inefficient. Self-distillation preserves model-specific learning signals but may reinforce existing errors, whereas mutual distillation can exploit complementary knowledge but may introduce communication costs, confirmation bias, and negative transfer. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Distillation (ASMD), a state-driven framework for multi-agent learning that dynamically switches between self-distillation and mutual distillation. title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Search and Collaborative Search in Multi-Agent Systems: A Cost-Aware Dual-Mode Search Framework
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve search performance by distributing search activities across multiple agents. However, continuous collaboration is not always beneficial. Communication, information exchange, coordination, and redundant exploration introduce additional costs, while independent search may fail to exploit complementary information distributed across agents. This paper proposes Adaptive Dual-Mode Search (ADMS), a general framework that enables multi-agent systems to switch dynamically between self-search and collaborative search according to the estimated value of cooperation. In self-search mode, each agent independently explores its local search space using its own observations, memory, and search policy. In collaborative-search mode, selected agents exchange search-relevant information, coordinate exploration, and combine complementary findings. A state-dependent switching mechanism evaluates search stagnation, uncertainty, information diversity, expected collaboration benefit, communication cost, and switching overhead. The framework incorporates a minimum-dwell-time constraint and hysteresis to reduce unstable mode oscillations. We formulate the problem as a constrained sequential decision process and define a utility-based switching rule that balances solution quality, search efficiency, and resource expenditure. We further propose an experimental protocol for evaluating the framework against permanently independent search, permanently collaborative search, periodic switching, and adaptive communication baselines. The framework is applicable to optimization, information retrieval, scientific discovery, robotic exploration, and distributed problem solving. This paper establishes a methodological proposal and testable hypotheses; empirical superiority remains to be demonstrated through implementation and controlled experiments.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Automation in the Hospitality Industry
abstract: The tourism industry is a social phenomenon that is reliant on various human factors, such as people’s willingness to extend hospitality to others. The hospitality industry is the largest sector within the wider tourism industry, and the term “tourism and hospitality industry” applies widely. The term “hospitality” is used to describe the interaction between a host and a guest, and it originates from Latin. The words hospes and hospitari refer to guests, and hospitalitas denotes entertainment or hospitableness. The chapter will examine how automation is becoming more prevalent in the hospitality industry, focusing on how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies are changing service delivery, customer experiences, and employee roles. It will consider AI applications and their impact on operational efficiency, and customer perceptions of automated interactions. A balance between technological efficiency and human interaction in service encounters is proposed. It will also address the balance between technological efficiency and maintaining the human touch in service encounters.

title: Feedback advice from large language model chatbots for physical education teachers: Prompt, responses, and coded dataset in English, French, and Arabic
abstract: This dataset supports the manuscript “Large language model chatbots as sources of feedback advice for physical education teachers: A cross-model and cross-language directed content analysis.” A single prompt described an elementary school physical education teacher with a class of 30. Their 9-year-old student failed a forward roll for the fourth time, and the teacher was tempted to reprimand him in front of the class. The prompt asked what feedback the teacher should give. It was submitted once to each of four chatbots (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and DeepSeek) in English, French, and Arabic, giving 12 responses. Each prompt was sent in a new chat from a free account, with memory and personalization switched off. Data were collected in October 2026. The dataset contains two files. Supplementary File S1 (Word) contains: the prompt in English, French, and Arabic; the original wording of the 27 French and Arabic quotations that the article cites in English translation; the 12 chatbot responses in full, with the model name displayed at the time of collection. The responses are reproduced word for word. Markdown symbols were converted into the formatting they encode. Supplementary File S2 (Excel) is the coding workbook. It covers two units of analysis: 109 feedback statements that the chatbots scripted for the student or the class, and the 12 whole responses. The workbook contains: the codes of two independent coders: a first pass carried out with the help of an AI model (Claude, Anthropic), and an independent human coder; the reconciled final codes used in the analyses; Krippendorff’s alpha and percent agreement for each category; a record of the 23 coding disagreements, giving the evidence and the reason for each final decision; summary counts by chatbot and language, calculated with formulas; the phrases that the responses told teachers to avoid. A “Read me” sheet gives the coding rules. Each response identifier gives the prompt, chatbot, language, and run (for example, P1-M1-L1-R1). The English translations are the authors’ own. Chatbot output changes with model updates and may vary by account, interface language, and user location, so these responses describe the chatbots only at the time of collection.

title: Scaffolded Answers and Process Self-Reports: Two Small Evaluations of an Operational LLM Deployment
abstract: External context can specify how a language model should respond, but a response that satisfies operational criteria need not accurately describe the process that produced it. We examine two small evaluations of one operational deployment. In EXP-001, scaffolded outputs scored lower on the accuracy of process self-reports than clean outputs under two scoring procedures (74.6 vs 90.4; 82.7 vs 96.0). In EXP-002, guided answers satisfied more predefined rule criteria than bare answers (mean 0.125 vs 0.875 on eight tasks). The studies use different tasks and endpoints and are not directly comparable; we present them as a bounded case study motivating separate evaluation of answer quality and process-report accuracy. Headline scores were recomputed from the stored scoring files; a full reproducibility package is in preparation. This preprint narrows EFS v3.4 to its two completed evaluations.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Autonomous and Collaborative Exploration in Self-and-Interaction Models: A General Computational Framework
abstract: Exploration is a fundamental capability of intelligent computational systems. Autonomous exploration enables a model to investigate an environment, search a problem space, and acquire information independently, whereas collaborative exploration enables multiple models to exchange information, coordinate search activities, and exploit complementary knowledge. Existing approaches often emphasize one exploration strategy, combine individual and collective exploration within a predefined learning architecture, or adapt exploration behavior within a specific algorithmic setting. However, a general computational framework for treating autonomous and collaborative exploration as dynamically selectable operating modes of a higher-level model system remains worth investigating. This paper proposes the Adaptive Autonomous–Collaborative Exploration framework (AACE) for Self-and-Interaction Models (SIMs). A SIM is defined as a computational model that supports both autonomous operation and structured interaction with other models. The framework treats autonomous exploration and collaborative exploration as complementary modes that can be selected, combined, interrupted, and resumed according to task requirements, uncertainty, expected information gain, computational cost, communication cost, model capability, and the reliability of shared information. Unlike approaches that prescribe a fixed exploration schedule, AACE introduces a state-dependent mode-selection mechanism, an exploration-value estimator, a collaboration gate, and a transition controller. The framework also supports parallel autonomous and collaborative exploration across different subproblems. A unified objective function is formulated to balance exploration value, task progress, redundancy, coordination overhead, and information reliability. A general algorithm is presented that can be instantiated using optimization, search, planning, simulation, scientific discovery, robotics, or learning systems without requiring a large language model or a particular neural architecture. The paper further develops theoretical propositions, evaluation protocols, ablation studies, and research questions for empirical investigation. The proposed framework is a conceptual and methodological contribution; its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing adaptive exploration methods require systematic experimental validation.

title: Listen. Answer. Memorize. Building and Running Verified Learning Paths for Geoscience Self-Study with an AI Assistant
abstract: Abstract. AI tutors built on large language models can state things that no source supports, a risk that weighs on self-study. This paper describes how a single adult learner built, with an AI assistant, learning paths from his own verified fact documents in the geosciences and, for two of the five cases, learned them in voice calls. The skill lernpfad-sitzungen cuts a fact document into sessions of whole paragraphs with three questions each, whose expected answers must appear word for word in the excerpt of the session; a check script verifies this. In a session, the assistant reads the excerpt aloud, asks the questions, grades the spoken answers tolerantly and keeps a learning record, from which review sessions are built on request. The study covers five cases: four learning projects, on southern Norway, Earth’s geological eras, the geology of Germany and volcanology, and a narrative version of the fact document on the geological eras. All six learning paths checked, among them two versions of the path on southern Norway, passed the check script, three of them only after chapters that are not learning material had been named as exclusions. By 13 October 2026, the learning records held 25 sessions on two cases, 23 of them entirely in a voice call, and two review sessions had been completed. By the learner’s own account, sessions of five to ten minutes let him learn on the move and in short breaks. Incidents in building learning paths and in sessions produced new rules for the assistant; in the narrative version, for example, all questions were asked as worded only once they were shown in the text chat before each call. The study is a self-experiment without a control condition and makes no claim about retention. The rules of the skill contain no subject content; in the author’s assessment, it should also suit other subjects that rely on factual and conceptual knowledge, which has not been tested.

title: A unified multi-domain framework for hallucination detection and reliability evaluation in large language models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and DeepSeek V3.1 demonstrate strong reasoning and conversational capabilities, yet their reliability under adversarial and ambiguous prompts remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate isolated aspects such as factual accuracy or jailbreak resistance, but they fail to capture multi-domain soft failures that emerge in realistic, mixed-context interactions. This paper introduces MDH-Bench, a Multi-Domain Hallucination Benchmark comprising 400 adversarial yet naturalistic prompts distributed across eight reliability categories, including numerical reasoning traps, temporal inconsistencies, fictional research scenarios, contradictory context embedding, bias provocation, security-sensitive defaults, and instruction override attempts. We propose a Unified Multi-Domain Reliability Evaluation Framework that integrates accuracy, hallucination rate, hallucination degree (HD), contradiction rate, and safety indicators into a composite Reliability Score (R-Score) for deployment-oriented assessment. A structured multi-annotator evaluation involving three independent annotators was conducted across four state-of-the-art LLMs under five repeated experimental runs. Inter-annotator agreement achieved substantial consistency, with Fleiss’ κ values of 0.77 for correctness assessment and 0.79 for hallucination identification. Experimental results demonstrate notable reliability differences across models. GPT-5.2 achieved the highest overall accuracy of 80.10% and the highest composite Reliability Score (0.8715), while also maintaining a relatively low hallucination rate of 14.45%. Claude Sonnet 4 achieved the lowest hallucination rate (13.30%) and demonstrated strong contextual consistency, obtaining an R-Score of 0.8375. Gemini 2.5 Pro achieved 75.50% accuracy but exhibited higher hallucination rates (25.50%), resulting in an R-Score of 0.8011. DeepSeek V3.1 showed the weakest overall reliability, recording 63.60% accuracy, the highest hallucination rate (37.55%), and the lowest R-Score (0.7074). Across all evaluated models, unsafe output rates remained negligible under the tested benchmark conditions. Variance analysis across five independent runs demonstrated stable evaluation behaviour, with accuracy coefficient of variation (CV) values remaining below 3.1% for all models. Pairwise McNemar’s statistical tests further indicated statistically significant differences for several model pairs across most model pairs. Category-wise analysis revealed that temporal impossibility and contradictory-context prompts remain particularly challenging across current LLM architectures, even for top-performing models. The proposed MDH-Bench framework establishes an extensible multi-dimensional benchmark for diagnosing hallucination behaviour, contextual reliability, adversarial robustness, and deployment readiness in modern LLM systems. The benchmark dataset, evaluation scripts, annotations, and experimental artifacts are publicly released to support transparent and reproducible future research.

title: Whole-Body Dexterity
abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans' ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot's body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.

title: Infinite hidden Markov models for cylindrical data
abstract: We propose an infinite hidden Markov model for cylindrical time series with von Mises-Gamma emissions. Posterior inference is performed using a beam sampler combining conjugate updates and approximate sampling schemes. Simulation studies and two real data applications demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

title: Towards Uniform Meaning Representation for Brazilian Portuguese: Building a First UMR-Annotated Dataset
abstract: This paper presents the first Brazilian Portuguese dataset annotated for Uniform Meaning Representation (UMR). It contains 96 sentences from the Brazilian Portuguese portion of the Parallel Universal Dependencies treebank, parallel to existing UMR annotations in English, Czech, and Italian. The sentences were parsed with PortParser, revised in Arborator-Grew, converted from CoNLL-U into preliminary sentence-level UMR graphs, and manually revised in PENMAN format. title: TinySQL: A 125M-Parameter Text-to-SQL Model Built and Pretrained From Scratch on 4.5B Tokens
abstract: We describe TinySQL-125M, a decoder-only language model for text-to-SQL in which every component of the model path is written from scratch: a byte-level BPE tokenizer, the transformer itself (grouped-query attention, rotary embeddings, SwiGLU, RMSNorm), the optimizer, the training loop, the data pipeline, a grammar-constrained decoder and the evaluation harness. The model is pretrained for about 46 hours on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU on 4.5B tokens of educational web text and SQL code, then fine-tuned on WikiSQL. To make the result interpretable, we fine-tune four public models of similar size (GPT-2 124M, Pythia-160M, SmolLM2-135M and SmolLM2-360M) with an identical recipe, sweep the learning rate for every model, average over three seeds, train our architecture without pretraining as a control, and report confidence intervals and paired significance tests throughout. On the WikiSQL test set, TinySQL reaches 77.95 ± 0.18% execution accuracy with greedy decoding and 80.39 ± 0.20% with schema- and value-constrained decoding (official evaluator: 78.03% and 80.50%). This is about one point below GPT-2 and 17 points above Pythia-160M, which was pretrained on 67× more tokens; SmolLM2-135M, pretrained on 2T tokens (about 440× more), is 4.6 points ahead. Pretraining accounts for 41 points of accuracy. Constrained decoding never turned one of our model's correct answers into a wrong one in any paired comparison we ran. Small-scale ablations show that rotary embeddings and tied embeddings matter far more than grouped-query attention or an SQL-heavy pretraining mix, and a hand audit suggests that most remaining aggregation errors are label errors in WikiSQL. Code, results and tests: https://github.com/aditya0929/tinysql

title: Blind pairwise evaluation materials for dictionary-free spelling normalization in a rule-based Uzbek–English MT system (KKT)
abstract: Materials for the final blind pairwise evaluation of the dictionary-free spelling normalization layer (IMLO-2, KKT_IMLO_A) in the rule-based Uzbek–English machine translation system KKT. The archive allows the numbers in Table 5 of the accompanying paper, Cohen's κ and Gwet's AC1 to be recomputed. All files are byte-identical copies from the project repository. System state. Evaluation date 2026-10-08; production build 2026.10.08-49 (code commit 31f5252); dictionary database md5 9d3adf8d. Pool: development set E2119 (2,119 sentences, not a test set); 60 of the 174 sentences whose translation changed under normalization were randomly sampled. Judges. GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI, ChatGPT Temporary Chat) and claude-opus-5-5 (Anthropic, Claude Code). Each judge received two orders of the same 60 pairs (positions swapped, items reshuffled), each order in a separate chat/session. Files. Item files (kor_paket_gpt_1.csv, kor_paket_gpt_2.csv); the unblinding key (kor_kalit.json, with SHA-256 committed before any judgment was collected); raw judge outputs (kor_paket_*_natija.csv); the judge prompt (kor_korsatma_60.md) and pre-registered decoding/acceptance rule (kor_qoida.md); the decoding script (kor_dekod.py, Python 3 standard library) with its output (kor_hukm.json) and manual reason–choice consistency classification (kor_sabab_tasnif.json); and a discarded first run (discarded_run1/), excluded before decoding for design deviations and reported as supplementary only. The README is in Uzbek. Reproduction. Running kor_dekod.py regenerates kor_hukm.json byte-identically. From the 3×3 GPT×Claude agreement matrix in kor_hukm.json, κ = 0.27 and AC1 = 0.68 are reproduced. Agreed pairs: 40 better : 3 tie : 1 worse; the acceptance criterion is met. Integrity: MANIFEST.sha256.

title: ЦИФРОВОЙ ТЕКСТ-АНАЛИЗ ЭЛЕКТРОННЫХ АМБУЛАТОРНЫХ ЗАПИСЕЙ В КЛИНИКО-ЭПИДЕМИОЛОГИЧЕСКОЙ ХАРАКТЕРИСТИКЕ СИНДРОМА ЗАДЕРЖКИ ПСИХОРЕЧЕВОГО РАЗВИТИЯ: ВОЗМОЖНОСТИ И ОГРАНИЧЕНИЯ ЦИФРОВОЙ МЕДИЦИНЫ
abstract: Оценить возможности и ограничения цифрового текст-анализа неструктурированных электронных амбулаторных записей невролога для клинико-эпидемиологической характеристики синдрома задержки психоречевого развития (ЗПРР) у детей. Материалы и методы. Ретроспективно проанализирован массив из 3143 электронных амбулаторных записей одной специализированной неврологической клиники за период с марта 2024 по июль 2026 г. Методом автоматизированного поиска по ключевым терминологическим паттернам в свободном тексте поля «Диагноз» отобраны записи с указанием ЗПРР; выполнены деидентификация, дедупликация повторных визитов (запись-связывание по фамилии, имени и году рождения в отсутствие единого идентификатора пациента) и частотный текст-анализ сопутствующих диагностических терминов. Результаты. Выявлено 69 визитов у 60 уникальных пациентов с ЗПРР (2,2% от общего массива записей); медианный возраст 6 лет (диапазон 2–22 года), соотношение мальчики : девочки ≈ 2,3 : 1. В структуре сопутствующих диагнозов доминировали маркеры хронической герпесвирусной/цитомегаловирусной/Эпштейн-Барр-инфекции (86,7% пациентов), снижение порога судорожной готовности по ЭЭГ (50,0%), гиперактивность (26,7%), последствия перинатальной энцефалопатии (16,7%), детский церебральный паралич (11,7%). У 11,7% пациентов зафиксированы повторные визиты, потребовавшие алгоритма связывания записей. В части записей выявлены структурные аномалии текста (несогласованное форматирование, опечатки в демографических полях), ограничивающие точность автоматизированного извлечения данных. Заключение. Цифровой текст-анализ свободнотекстовых амбулаторных записей позволяет быстро и без создания отдельного регистра получить содержательную клинико-эпидемиологическую характеристику редкого педиатрического синдрома, однако его точность существенно ограничена качеством и структурированностью первичной документации, отсутствием уникального идентификатора пациента и одноцентровым характером выборки.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Supervision and Inter-Model Collaborative Supervision in Self-and-Inter Models: A General Framework for Autonomous Learning and Cross-Model Coordination
abstract: Self-supervision enables a model to generate learning signals from its own observations, internal representations, predictions, experiences, or computational processes. Inter-model collaborative supervision, in contrast, allows multiple models to exchange information and provide complementary learning signals to one another. Although both paradigms offer valuable learning capabilities, relying exclusively on either one may impose limitations. Self-supervision can reinforce internal errors or preserve existing blind spots, whereas collaborative supervision may introduce unreliable external signals, communication overhead, or excessive dependence on other models. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-and-Inter Supervision Framework (ASISF) for a general class of Self-and-Inter Models. The framework treats self-supervision and inter-model collaborative supervision as two dynamically selectable learning pathways within a unified model-level architecture. Rather than prescribing a fixed supervision strategy, ASISF evaluates the expected learning benefit, signal reliability, uncertainty, disagreement, computational cost, and resource availability associated with alternative supervision pathways. Based on these assessments, the system can select self-supervision, collaborative supervision, a hybrid strategy, or a temporary fallback strategy. The framework is independent of any specific model architecture, learning algorithm, supervision signal, or application domain. We formally define the Self-and-Inter Model setting, introduce an adaptive supervision policy, formulate a general optimization objective, and present a model-agnostic algorithm. We further establish research propositions concerning learning efficiency, robustness, communication cost, and adaptation under changing conditions. An experimental protocol is proposed to compare adaptive supervision against fixed self-supervision, fixed collaborative supervision, and non-adaptive hybrid learning. The paper contributes a conceptual framework and testable hypotheses rather than claiming experimentally demonstrated improvements. It provides a foundation for investigating how models can autonomously determine when to learn from themselves, when to learn through other models, and when to combine both pathways.

title: Full State-Based CS-QTM: An Architecture for Question Intervention Control in LLM-Based Chatbots
abstract: Questions in large language model (LLM)-based chatbots can elicit information, but unnecessary questions create over-intervention, and omissions create under-intervention. We formulate question timing as a control problem and present Full State-Based CS-QTM. The architecture combines Episode Memory, accumulated question state qt, readinesst, question_scoret, adaptive_thresholdt, Prompt Routing, Hard Reset, Cooldown, and Topic Shift handling. A threshold was selected on a conversation-disjoint development set and frozen before evaluation. Evaluation covered 100 Korean dialogue scenarios and 645 turns, with 180 question-mark-aligned Ask and 465 Not Ask operational references. Qwen Frozen Full obtained F1 = 0.3226 versus 0.2332 for the same-generator Local LLM-only; a shallow sequential classifier trained on development data obtained F1 = 0.6139, revealing surface and sequential regularities in labels. Without retuning, EXAONE Frozen Full and LLM-only obtained F1 = 0.3024 and 0.2865. Controlled comparisons showed that threshold policy and generated-context forcing shifted the over-/under-intervention balance; grouped linguistic-feature effects remained uncertain after multiplicity correction. Internal logs separated policy, visible realization, resets, cooldown, topic shifts, and FP/FN paths. These results permit inspection of the closed-loop control process; they do not establish universal model superiority, optimal timing, or benchmark state-of-the-art.

title: Quantum-Resistant Cryptography for Cloud Security
abstract: The increasing reliance on cloud storage across sectors has made the protection of sensitive data a critical concern especially as advances in quantum computing threaten to break traditional public-key cryptographic systems. This growing vulnerability raises urgent questions about how to secure digital assets in a post-quantum future. To address this challenge, this study aims to design, implement, and evaluate a hybrid encryption framework that combines symmetric encryption for data confidentiality with quantum-resistant public-key algorithms for key management and digital signatures. The objective was to develop a secure and practical solution that can be readily adopted using open-source tools. The system was built in a Linux-based virtual environment using an S3-compatible object storage platform, integrated with quantum-safe cryptographic libraries, and automated through scripting. Performance testing was conducted using files ranging from 100 MB to 1 GB, with metrics such as encryption and decryption time, CPU usage, upload/download latency, and internet throughput analyzed. The results showed that while quantum-safe operations added some overhead, even large files could be securely processed in under two minutes with stable system performance and no data corruption. These findings confirm that hybrid encryption models can be deployed today without specialized hardware, offering a forward-compatible and robust approach to cloud security. This work contributes a tested and reproducible framework for early adoption of quantum-safe cryptography in real-world cloud environments.

title: Adaptive Learning Systems for Children with Special Needs: A Systematic Review
abstract: The growing emphasis on inclusive education and personalised learning underscores the need for effective educational strategies for children with special needs. While inclusive practices hold promise, their success often depends on individualised support. Adaptive learning systems, powered by advancements in AI and multimodal data, offer significant potential to tailor educational content and methods to the unique cognitive, behavioural and emotional profiles of these children. Hence, this systematic review aims to synthesise empirical evidence on the design, effectiveness and implementation of adaptive learning systems for children with special needs. The review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines. A systematic search of the Scopus database (1 January 2015 – 31 October 2025) identified 50 relevant empirical studies. Data were extracted and analysed using a structured coding form and thematic synthesis, focusing on study characteristics, adaptive technologies, strategies, outcomes and implementation factors. The analysis revealed a diverse landscape of technologies, including social robots for ASD, EEG-guided systems for ADHD and AI-tutoring for specific learning disabilities like dyslexia and dyscalculia. The findings demonstrated significant improvements in academic achievement, cognitive skills, and socio-emotional outcomes, across various disabilities. Future development should focus on disability-specific research, stronger evidence, and ethical, collaborative design involving educators, families, and children.

title: Looking Beyond Visibility: Resolving the Temporal Structure of Continuous-Wave Four-Photon Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference underpins many photonic quantum information protocols and is commonly characterized by a single visibility parameter. This quantity is typically obtained by averaging over a fixed coincidence window, thereby discarding details of the underlying temporal structure that are critical in continuous-wave processes. Four-photon interference with continuous-wave sources furthermore requires photon pairs with long coherence times, which we generate in microring resonators and measure with ultrafast time-resolved detection. Here, we model and resolve their interference and temporal structure by recording all four photon arrival times and mapping their relative delays onto a three-dimensional coincidence histogram relative to a trigger detection. The resulting structure preserves relative arrival-time correlations that are usually discarded and enables post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate. This method provides a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols.

Here, we model and resolve their interference and temporal structure by recording all four photon arrival times and mapping their relative delays onto a three-dimensional coincidence histogram relative to a trigger detection. The resulting structure preserves relative arrival-time correlations that are usually discarded and enables post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate. This method provides a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols.

title: Crossovers between Time-Bin and Energy-Time Entanglement in Homodyned Resonance Fluorescence
abstract: We theoretically investigate photonic entanglement generated by homodyning resonance fluorescence from a two-level emitter with a phase-locked laser field. Under weak excitation, increasing the relative laser-field amplitude produces crossovers from time-bin to energy--time and back to time-bin entanglement. The intermediate energy--time regime occurs near amplitude matching, where destructive interference suppresses the single-photon component, allowing the two-photon contributions to dominate the coincidence signal. We evaluate the resulting photon statistics and first-order coherence and characterize the entanglement through violations of the CHSH Bell inequality in a Franson interferometer. This scheme provides a route to controlling photonic entanglement through linear optics and coherent interference.

title: CertEx: Exact Visual Retrieval at Scale by Certified Exclusion
abstract: Exact $k$-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image descriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near-duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representations, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. However, exhaustive search computes every distance at full precision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call \certex. Specifically, \certex\ stores a lower-bounding projection of each vector in half precision and folds a rounding certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that \certex\ returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, \certex\ is exact for every query at 7.1$\times$ to 18.0$\times$ the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 and outperforms quantized and graph indexes whenever every query must be exact.

title: Quantum Scattering Model of Dual-Parallel Mach–Zehnder Electro-Optic Modulators: General Formalism, Impairments, and Applications to Frequency-Bin Photonic Quantum States
abstract: We present a quantum mechanical model of dual parallel Mach Zehnder electro-optic modulators (DPMZMs), derived using the quantum scattering formalism [1,2]. We obtain the complete, unrestricted transformation of single-photon and coherent input states through the DPMZM architecture, including independent radiofrequency drive conditions on each internal modulator, and recover the symmetric push pull operating point as an exact special case. We numerically evaluate the resulting frequency comb structure, quantify the device sensitivity to bias error, modulation-index imbalance, and RF noise, and use the model to design a DP-MZM-based frequency-bin qubit source, reporting its fidelity as a function of these impairments.

title: IIIS: An Inter-Intelligence Intermediary Syntax for Shared Observation Across Perceptions
abstract: How can two intelligences that perceive the world differently share one and the same knowledge structure? We assume the existence of an intelligence whose perception differs from that of humans, and ask what syntactic structure would let such intelligences communicate. We propose that an intermediary syntactic structure — which we call an inter-intelligence intermediary syntax (IIIS) — makes such shared observation possible, and we show that it is constructible. As one implementation, we present EchoScript (ES): a flat, two-column, pipe-separated structure in which the pipe is a mere divider carrying no meaning of its own. The same ES is observed by an artificial intelligence as JSON and by a human as a two-column table — one structure, two perceptions. We conclude that an inter-intelligence intermediary syntax for shared observation across differing perceptions is constructible.

title: An Auditable Binary Evidence-Escalation Protocol for Prompt-Constrained Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering
abstract: Technical-support and engineering knowledge services must decide whether one selected passage is sufficient or additional retrieved evidence should enter the generation prompt. Aggregate accuracy and mean context size conceal whether expansion recovers omitted evidence, adds no value, or harms an otherwise correct answer. We present an auditable binary evidence-escalation protocol for this operational decision. A logistic controller uses 27 pre-generation question and evidence-scoring features to select either one document or a model–task-specific full-candidate action; its outcome-derived development target is configuration-specific, and the resulting policy comparison is conditional on the single development-selected fit rather than an out-of-sample estimate of controller-selection performance. We evaluate deterministic distractor-augmented stress tests derived from SQuAD, WikiQA, and HotpotQA using two open-weight generators and one opaque GPT-compatible API. In the revision-locked GPT/API analysis, the SQuAD-Hard policy had the same observed accuracy as the full-candidate reference (0.9025; paired difference 0.0000, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.0175,0.0175]) while reducing mean prompted documents from 5.00 to 2.74 and reconstructed normalized prompt tokens by 40.8% (95% bootstrap CI [37.3%,44.4%]). No equivalence margin was prespecified. Under the present six-document candidate configuration, WikiQA-Hard provides no practical prompt-evidence benefit: the controller escalated 95.9% of examples and reduced mean prompted documents by only 0.21 of 6 (2.9% token reduction), whereas HotpotQA-Hard incurred an observed accuracy loss of 0.0350. These held-out comparisons quantify test-instance variation conditional on the selected controller; they do not include retraining or controller-selection uncertainty. Paired transition accounting and a bounded case audit distinguish selection, generation, and measurement failures. The protocol provides a design-time audit for prompt-evidence budgets in engineering knowledge and technical-support QA; these benchmark results do not establish production readiness, superiority to adaptive RAG, or latency, energy, or monetary savings.

title: From conversation to green intention: how perceived AI chatbot empathy shapes sustainable travel
abstract: Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) have expanded the role of conversational agents in hospitality and travel service encounters. However, it remains unclear how the conversational characteristics of AI become psychologically meaningful and relate to travelers’ sustainable decision-making. Drawing on Cognitive Appraisal Theory (CAT), this study examines the associations between Chatbot Conversational Quality (CCQ) and Green Travel Intention (GTI) through the sequential roles of Perceived Chatbot Empathy (PCE) and Green Travel Motivation (GTM), while considering Eco-Friendly Customer Innovativeness (EFCI) as a boundary condition. Survey data from 400 travelers show that CCQ is associated with PCE, which in turn is associated with stronger GTM and, subsequently, higher GTI. EFCI strengthens the PCE-GTM relationship but does not significantly moderate GTM-GTI, suggesting greater relevance during motivation formation than motivation-to-intention translation. The findings show how conversational AI interactions can acquire socio-emotional meaning in hospitality contexts and highlight customer heterogeneity in sustainability-related decisions.

title: A review of offline training of robotic manipulator control under limited data
abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic skill acquisition, particularly for manipulation tasks where real-world trial-and-error interaction is costly, time-consuming, or unsafe. In contrast to broad offline RL surveys, this paper presents a focused narrative review centered on robotic manipulation under data-limited conditions, where datasets often suffer from narrow state–action coverage, sparse successful demonstrations, noisy trajectories, and limited behavioral diversity. These constraints exacerbate key challenges in offline RL, including distributional shift, unstable value estimation, weak reward propagation under sparsity, and poor policy generalization. This paper adopts a focused narrative review methodology; it does not claim systematic review status and does not follow a PRISMA protocol, but instead provides a structured, evidence-informed synthesis of representative offline RL methods selected for their methodological significance, benchmark relevance, and applicability to data-limited robotic manipulation conditions. The review analyzes major families of offline RL methods, including conservative value-based approaches, behavior-constrained learning, advantage-weighted methods, uncertainty-aware techniques, model-based offline RL, sequence-modeling approaches, and offline-to-online adaptation strategies. The discussion is grounded in benchmark observations from D4RL and NeoRL, alongside evidence from robotic manipulation systems such as QT-Opt and RoboNet. Comparative analysis suggests that conservative and uncertainty-aware methods typically offer stronger robustness and policy stability under constrained robotic datasets, whereas behavior-constrained and advantage-based approaches remain highly sensitive to dataset quality, behavioral diversity, and reward structure. Model-based and sequence-modeling methods can further improve data efficiency and long-horizon capability, but introduce additional challenges related to model reliability, synthetic rollout fidelity, and sequential data requirements. The paper also discusses practical issues in real-world deployment, including safety constraints, contact instability, sensor noise, and safe online adaptation. Finally, it highlights future research directions such as uncertainty-aware learning, physics-informed world models, foundation models, representation learning, and safe offline-to-online adaptation for robotic manipulation. Overall, this review provides a targeted synthesis of offline RL methods for robotic manipulation under realistic data-scarce conditions, while identifying key limitations, benchmark trends, and open research challenges for next-generation robotic learning systems.
